source_text: In illud: Non potest filius a se facere Ἀμφιλοχίου ἐπισκόπου Ἰκονίου <ἐκ τοῦ εἰς τὸ Οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν> ... Τὸ Οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν, πῶς νοεῖτε; Τὸ γὰρ οὐ δύναται κατὰ δύο τρόπους ἐκλαμβάνετε· καὶ κατὰ τὴν κοινὴν χρῆσιν καὶ κατὰ τὴν θείαν γραφήν. Λέγεται γὰρ τὸ οὐ δύναται καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἀδυνάτων καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν μὴ ἐγχωρούντων· ἄλλο δὲ τὸ μὴ δύνασθαι καὶ ἄλλο τὸ μὴ ἐγχωρεῖν. Περὶ μὲν τῶν ἀδυνάτων ὁ Παῦλος οὕτω λέγει· Ἀδύνατον αἷμα ταύρων καὶ τράγων περιελεῖν ἁμαρτίας· αἷμα γὰρ ἀλόγου λογικῆς ψυχῆς οὐ καθαίρει πάθη. Περὶ δὲ τῶν μὴ ἐγχωρούντων ἐν ταῖς Πράξεσιν οἱ ἀπόστολοι· Οὐ δυνάμεθα, φησίν, ἡμεῖς ἃ εἴδομεν καὶ ἠκούσαμεν μὴ λαλεῖν· καὶ μὴν ἠδύναντο μὴ λαλεῖν ἀλλ' οὐκ ἠνείχοντο σιωπᾶν, ἵνα μὴ δόξωσιν ἀρνεῖσθαι τοῦ θαυματουργοῦντος τὴν χάριν. Εἴπατε οὖν ἐνταῦθα, τὸ Οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν, κατὰ ποῖον ἐκλαμβάνετε τρόπον· ἀδυναμίαν αὐτοῦ καταψηφιζόμενοι ἢ τῆς αὐτεξουσίου γνώμης ἀναιροῦντες τὰ κινήματα, ὅτι ὅσα θέλει δύναται. Ἀλλὰ τί λέγεις· ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐ ποιεῖ, ἀλλὰ πρόσταγμα θεοῦ πληρῶν ἐκεῖνα ἐργάζεται εἰς ὅπερ ἂν τὸ τοῦ προστάξαντος νεῦμα βλέπῃ; Καὶ πῶς οὐκ ἔστιν ἐσχάτης ἀνοίας τοῦτο λέγειν· εἰ γὰρ ὁλῶς οὐδὲν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ ποιεῖ, οὔτε γνώμῃ τὴν οἰκονομίαν ὅλην ἐπλήρωσεν οὔτε συμπαθείᾳ τῇ πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὴν ἡμῶν ἀνέλαβε σάρκα οὔτε φιλίᾳ αὐθαίρετον τὸν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατεδέξατο θάνα τον, ἀλλὰ πάντα βίᾳ ὑπέμεινεν ὑπὸ τῆς ἀνάγκης συνωθούμενος. Εἰ δὲ τολμηρὸν καὶ βλάσφημον καὶ πάσης ἀσεβείας ἐπέκεινα τὸ τοῦτο εἰπεῖν, εἴπατε ἡμῖν κατὰ ποῖον λόγον τὸ Οὐ δύναται ὁ υἱὸς ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ τι ποιεῖν ἐκλαμβάνετε. Ὅτι γάρ, κἂν μὴ θέλητε, λέγετε δύνασθαι αὐτὸν ποιεῖν ἅπερ βούλεται, ὑπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐλαυνό μενοι δῆλον. Ἀλλὰ τί περίττους ὑφαίνω λόγους; Λύει γὰρ τὸ ζήτημα ἡ ἐπαγωγὴ τοῦ ῥητοῦ· οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν ὅτι Οὐ δύναται ποιεῖν ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν, ἐὰν μή τι προστάξῃ ὁ πατήρ, ἀλλ' ἐὰν μὴ βλέπῃ τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα· ἐὰν δὲ ἴδῃ αὐτὸν ποιοῦντά τι, ταῦτα καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ. Οὐκοῦν οὐ λειτουργίαν πληρῶν ποιεῖ ἅπερ προσ τάττει ὁ πατήρ, ἀλλ' ὡς ὅμοιος, ὡς ἰσοδύναμος, ὡς τῆς αὐτῆς θείας φύσεως ὤν· ἅπερ ἂν ἴδῃ τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα, ταῦτα καὶ ὁ υἱὸς ὁμοίως ποιεῖ. Μετὰ ταῦτα, φησίν, ἦν ἡ ἑορτὴ τῶν Ἰουδαίων καὶ ἀνέβη Ἰησοῦς εἰς τὰ Ἱεροσόλυμα. Ἵνα δὲ μὴ τοῖς ὕδασι ἐπιγράψωσι τὸ πᾶν, οὐ πρότερον ἰᾶτο τὰ ὕδατα πρὶν ἄγγελος αὐτὰ ἐπιστὰς ἐσάλευσεν, ἵνα μάθωσιν ὡς οὔτε τὰ ὕδατα τοῦ βαπτίσματος καθ' ἑαυτὰ ὀνίνησι τὴν ψυχὴν πρὶν ἂν ὁ μεγάλης βουλῆς ἄγγελος ἀνθρώπινον ὑποδὺς σῶμα ἐπὶ τὸ βάπτισμα ἔλθῃ. Πολλῶν οὖν ἀσθενῶν ὄντων ἔκειτο καὶ παραλυτικὸς ἀνὴρ ὀκτὼ καὶ τριάκοντα ἔτη ἔχων ἐν τῇ ἀσθενείᾳ, ὃν ἰδὼν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐρωτᾷ· Θέλεις ὑγιὴς γενέσθαι;
thought_title: Two senses of “cannot” and the Son’s seeing the Father
orientation: Amphilochius opens his homily on John 5:19 by asking his hearers how they understand the phrase “the Son cannot do anything of himself,” distinguishing two senses of “cannot” before turning to the Gospel scene at the pool.
pass_a_gloss: On the saying: The Son cannot do anything of himself, by Amphilochius bishop of Iconium, from the work on “The Son cannot do anything of himself.” The saying “The Son cannot do anything of himself,” how do you understand it? For the “cannot” you take in two ways: both according to common usage and according to the divine Scripture. For “cannot” is said both of impossible things and of things not permitted; and one thing is not being able, and another thing is not being permitted. Concerning impossible things Paul speaks thus: It is impossible for blood of bulls and goats to take away sins; for blood of an irrational animal does not cleanse the passions of a rational soul. Concerning things not permitted, in Acts the apostles say: We cannot, they say, not speak what we saw and heard; and indeed they were able not to speak, but they did not endure to be silent, lest they seem to deny the grace of the wonder-worker. Tell us then here, the saying “The Son cannot do anything of himself,” according to which way do you take it? Do you vote condemnation of his inability, or do you remove the movements of his self-determined will, because whatever he wishes he can do? But what do you say: he does not do of himself, but fulfilling a command of God he works those things toward whatever the nod of the one commanding looks? And how is it not of extreme folly to say this? For if he does absolutely nothing of himself, neither by his own will did he fulfill the whole plan of salvation, nor by compassion toward us did he take up our flesh, nor by love did he accept of his own choice the death on our behalf, but he endured all things by force, driven together by necessity. But if it is daring and blasphemous and beyond all impiety to say this, tell us according to what reasoning you take the saying “The Son cannot do anything of himself.” For that, even if you do not wish it, you say that he can do whatever he wants, driven by the truth, is clear. But why do I weave superfluous words? For the continuation of the saying solves the question; for he did not say that “He cannot do anything of himself, unless the Father commands something,” but “unless he sees the Father doing”; and if he sees him doing something, these things the Son also does in the same way. Therefore he does not do what the Father commands by fulfilling a service, but as one like, as one equal in power, as one being of the same divine nature; whatever he sees the Father doing, these things the Son also does in the same way. After these things, it says, there was the feast of the Jews and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. And lest they ascribe everything to the waters, the waters did not heal before an angel standing over them stirred them, so that they might learn that neither do the waters of baptism by themselves benefit the soul before the angel of great counsel, putting on a human body, comes to baptism. Therefore while many sick were lying there, there also lay a paralytic man having thirty-eight years in the sickness, whom Jesus seeing asks: Do you wish to become well?

choices.why: The glossary requires “cannot” for this phrase, and the homily's whole argument turns on distinguishing senses of this exact wording.
The glossary requires “of himself” for this phrase, which is central to the argument about independent action.
The glossary requires “in the same way” to convey that the Son does the same works in the same manner as the Father, not merely similar works.
The glossary gives “service” for διακονίαν; here λειτουργίαν carries the same sense of ministerial subordination that Amphilochius denies of the Son.

choices.english: being of the same divine nature
choices.why: The glossary requires “nature” for φύσις; the phrase expresses the Son's consubstantiality with the Father, which is the homily's theological point.
rejected: being of the same divine essence
being of the same divine substance

choices.why: Amphilochius contrasts ἀδύνατα with μὴ ἐγχωροῦντα; “not permitted” captures the sense of what is unfitting or not allowed rather than strictly impossible.

pass_b_english: “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19)—how do you understand this? You take the word “cannot” in two ways, both in common usage and in the divine Scripture. “Cannot” is said both of things that are impossible and of things that are not permitted. Not being able is one thing; not being permitted is another. About impossible things Paul speaks this way: “The blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4). For the blood of an irrational animal does not cleanse the passions of a rational soul. About things not permitted, the apostles say in Acts: “We cannot,” they say, “stop speaking about what we have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20). And yet they were unable to stop speaking, for they could not bear to be silent, lest they seem to deny the grace of the one who worked wonders.

So tell me here: when you hear “The Son can do nothing of himself,” in which way do you take it? Do you condemn him as weak, or do you deny the movements of his free will, since he can do whatever he wills? But what do you say—that he does nothing of himself, but fulfills God’s command and works at whatever the nod of the one commanding directs? How is it not utter foolishness to say this? For if he does absolutely nothing of himself, then he neither fulfilled the whole plan of salvation by his own will, nor took up our flesh out of compassion for us, nor accepted death for our sake by his own free love, but endured everything by force, driven by necessity.

If it is reckless and blasphemous and beyond all impiety to say that, then tell me in what sense you understand “The Son can do nothing of himself.” For it is clear—even if you do not want it—that you are driven by the truth to say he can do whatever he wishes. But why do I spin out unnecessary words? The continuation of the saying resolves the question. For he did not say, “He can do nothing of himself unless the Father commands something,” but “unless he sees the Father doing.” And whatever he sees him doing, these things the Son also does in the same way. So he does not do what the Father commands by fulfilling a service, but as one like him, as one equal in power, as one who is of the same divine nature: whatever he sees the Father doing, these things the Son also does in the same way.

After this, he says, there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem (John 5:1). And so that they would not attribute everything to the waters, the waters did not heal before an angel stood over them and stirred them, so that they might learn that the waters of baptism do not benefit the soul by themselves before the angel of great counsel, putting on a human body, comes to baptism. So while many sick people were lying there, a paralyzed man was there as well, who had been ill for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him, he asks him: “Do you want to be made well?” (John 5:5-6).

problems.quote: And yet they were able to stop speaking, but they could not bear to be silent
problems.source_quote: καὶ μὴν ἠδύναντο μὴ λαλεῖν … ἵνα μὴ δόξωσιν ἀρνεῖσθαι τὸν θαυματουργοῦντα τὴν χάριν
problems.why: The source says the apostles could not refrain from speaking (they were unable to stop speaking); the English reverses this, saying they were able to stop speaking.
problems.fix: And yet they were unable to stop speaking, for they could not bear to be silent, lest they seem to deny the grace of the one who worked wonders.
problems.ruling: Source ἠδύναντο μὴ λαλεῖν means 'they were able not to speak'; English reverses to 'able to stop speaking' (i.e., able to refrain), which contradicts the Greek. The Greek says they had the ability to not speak, but chose not to exercise it. The English mistranslation inverts the meaning: 'able to stop speaking' vs. 'able not to speak' are logically different, and the context shows the apostles had the physical ability to remain silent but were compelled by conscience to speak. The English misleads readers about the rhetorical point.

edits.old: And yet they were able to stop speaking, but they could not bear to be silent
edits.new: And yet they were unable to stop speaking, for they could not bear to be silent

fixed: The source says 'καὶ μὴν ἠδύναντο μὴ λαλεῖν ἀλλ' οὐκ ἠνείχοντο σιωπᾶν' — 'and indeed they were able not to speak, but they did not endure to be silent.' The English 'they were able to stop speaking' misreads the construction: 'μὴ λαλεῖν' means 'not to speak,' so 'ἠδύναντο μὴ λαλεῖν' means 'they were able not to speak' (i.e., they had the capacity to remain silent), but the following clause 'ἀλλ' οὐκ ἠνείχοντο σιωπᾶν' ('but they did not endure to be silent') explains why they did not exercise that capacity. The English 'they were able to stop speaking' reverses the sense by suggesting they could stop, whereas the source says they could not bear to be silent. Changed to 'they were unable to stop speaking, for they could not bear to be silent' to match the source's contrast between capacity and endurance.
